opus-5.5.text:
Looking back, it's a little funny, because at the time it felt like a side project, almost a detour from what I thought the "real" research was. During rotations you're supposed to be exploring, trying things out, figuring out which lab and which problems fit you. I got excited about the idea that if we want robots to learn the way people do, we should be looking at how people actually see and act in the world, from their own point of view.

So the system was pretty scrappy: a headset, some tracking, a lot of duct-tape engineering to get the streams synchronized and make the data usable. Honestly, a lot of the time went into unglamorous things like calibration, latency, and figuring out why the hand poses were drifting. But I learned a lot from that. Data collection isn't a solved preliminary step you rush through; the interface you build to capture demonstrations shapes what your models can learn.

What strikes me now is how much the field has come back around to that idea. Today everyone talks about scaling human data, egocentric video, teleoperation interfaces, and using human demonstrations as a foundation for robot learning. Back then it was a niche interest, and the hardware and the learning methods weren't quite ready to make it pay off at scale. So I'd describe it as being a bit early rather than wrong.

If I could tell my younger self something, it would be to take that kind of infrastructure work more seriously and not treat it as secondary. Some of the most lasting contributions in our field come from people who built the tools that made the data possible, not just the algorithms on top. That rotation planted a seed that has stayed with me through my later work on imitation learning and on learning from human data.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, with a lot of fondness, and a little bit of embarrassment at how naive I was about what the hard part would be.

So the context was my first year at Stanford, doing rotations before I settled into Fei-Fei's lab. I was coming in with this conviction that the bottleneck for robot learning was data, and specifically human data. Robots are expensive, slow, and they break. Humans are everywhere and they do manipulation effortlessly. So the idea was, what if we just instrument a person? Put a headset on them, capture the egocentric view, track the hands, and get a firehose of demonstrations that we could later turn into robot policies.

And I spent a lot of that rotation basically doing hardware and systems work. Calibrating cameras, fighting with tracking jitter, writing the pipeline to sync everything. I think I came out of it with a pretty good system for the time, and we actually collected a decent amount of data.

What I look back on now is that the system was never really the bottleneck. The bottleneck was the gap between what a human does and what a robot can do. A person's hand is doing a thousand tiny things, compliance in the fingers, subtle wrist adjustments, that the robot just can't replicate. So you'd have beautiful demonstrations that were kind of useless because the embodiment was so different. That problem, the embodiment gap, is something I've been chasing in one form or another ever since.

The other thing it taught me, which I didn't appreciate at the time, is that collecting data is a research problem, not an engineering chore. How you capture, what you capture, what the interface is, all of that shapes what you can learn later. I used to think of it as the boring part you get through before the real ML. Now I think it's half the problem.

So, was it a success? The paper outcome was modest. But I'd say it set the whole direction of my research. A lot of what I think about today, scaling up demonstrations, building better interfaces for humans to teach robots, learning from heterogeneous data, that all traces back to a first-year student sitting in a lab with a VR headset that kept drifting.

astra-6.text:
I look back on it as an early attempt to understand how we could capture human behavior in a form that would be useful for robots. The appeal of an egocentric setup was that you could see the task from the person’s perspective, and VR gave us a way to explore that interaction.

But capturing data and making that data useful for learning are two different problems. You have to think about what the system observes, what information is missing, and how a human’s actions relate to what a robot can actually do. For me, that’s the interesting lens to look back through: the capture system is one piece, but the bigger question is how you bridge human experience and robot learning.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back, I think of it as an early exploration of how we could get useful human demonstrations for robots. During my Stanford PhD rotations, I built a system around egocentric capture and VR, trying to connect what a person sees and does with the information a robot would need to learn a task.

The interesting challenge was that capturing human behavior and turning it into useful robot data are different problems. A demonstration can look perfectly natural to us, but you still have to work out what matters for the task and how that transfers to a robot with a different body. That experience pushed me to think about data collection and robot learning together: what do you need to capture so that a demonstration actually helps the robot learn?
